newsitem.title: UK: British minister reopens Conservatives' EU wounds.
newsitem.headline: British minister reopens Conservatives' EU wounds.

text.p: Newspapers accused a member of Prime Minister John Major's cabinet on Friday of jockeying for position ahead of a post-election Conservative leadership battle by adopting a more sceptical stance towards Europe.
Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell, once on the pro-European wing of the ruling party, called on Thursday for Britain to negotiate a new relationship with its European Union partners.
His call delighted the party's right wing. "It shows how far the Conservative Party has turned against Europe," one member of parliament, Rhodes Boyson, told Sky television .

It also suggested that the arrival of general election year -- Major must call polls by May 22 -- had failed to moderate Conservative feuding over Europe which for months has marred their electoral prospects.

"We need to negotiate with our partners a relationship into the next century which reflects the reality of the next century -- that is to say the need to win in a much more flexible and competitive market place," Dorrell said.

The Times said the statement by the once strong pro-European was "a display of ambition too naked for this chill January. It is a crude attempt by Mr Dorrell to position himself for a Tory (Conservative) leadership election."

The Express said: "Mr Dorrell may well be preparing for the leadership race which will follow a Tory election defeat...He is also conceding that he sees which way the wind is blowing in the Tory Party."

Labour deputy leader John Prescott agreed that Dorrell was preparing a bid for power. "He has jumped ship and now wants to get in the race. For that in the Tory Party, you have to be against the present line," he said.
Major is widely expected to step down as leader if the Conservatives, some 20 points behind the Labour Party in the polls, are forced out of power for the first time in almost 18 years.

Potential contenders in a battle to replace him range from pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke to John Redwood, a right-winger who quit the cabinet in 1995 to challenge Major for the leadership.
Pro-European Conservative MP Quentin Davies, in an apparent attack on Dorrell, warned against a "purely cynical move to change policy for electoral reasons."
"There's no question of turning the European Union into some kind of free trade area, and any idea of that kind is quite unrealistic, and indeed would be idiotic," he said.
In an article in the Daily Telegraph, Major insisted that his party was united on fundamental principles such as the need to preserve family values and traditional institutions.
"Whatever our sincerely-held differences may be on particular issues, those of us who are drawn to the Conservative cause know the power of the bonds that bind us together," he said.
